lesson_title: Relationships, Tables and Formulae: Finding the Rule in a Bill
hook_text: The plumber charges you before he even opens his toolbox. Here's how to read that bill like a maths teacher.
clip_script: The plumber walks into your yard and you already owe R350. That's the call-out. Then the clock starts: R280 an hour. One hour, R630. Two hours, R910. Three hours, R1 190. Look at the jumps — R280, R280, R280. Same jump every time. That's your rule: something fixed at the start, something extra per unit. Now the flip side. You hire a bakkie for R1 800 and split it. Alone, R1 800. Two of you, R900. Three, R600. Six, R300. The bakkie never got cheaper — it just got shared further. Multiply people by price every time and you always land on R1 800. And here's the one that pays you back: the water bill says R790. R145 of that is the basic charge, before a single tap opens. Take it off first — R645 left. Divide by R21,50 a kilolitre — thirty kilolitres. Take the fixed part off FIRST, every time. Divide the whole R790 and you'll be out by nearly seven kilolitres and a whole mark.
visual_style: A kitchen table stacked with real South African bills — a plumber's invoice, a municipal water statement — with the fixed charge circled in one colour and the per-unit rate in another; numbers lifting off the paper into a table and then a straight line.
mood: Calm, streetwise, the voice of someone who has paid these bills.
pacing: Steady through the plumber, quicker through the bakkie split, slow and deliberate on the reverse calculation.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never guess at a tariff again.
